about.metaTitle: About — the agency and its founder
about.metaDescription: RAPIA is the artificial intelligence division of Rapyogo SARL, a Congolese group based in Goma. Michel Bengana's background, verifiable recognitions, and what we refuse to publish.
about.heading: Who is behind RAPIA
about.subtitle: A Congolese agency backed by a group that runs its own products — and would rather say what it cannot do than let you assume otherwise.
agencyBody: RAPIA is the artificial intelligence division of Rapyogo SARL, a company incorporated under Congolese law and registered in Goma. It operates from three locations — Goma, Kinshasa, Lubumbashi — with companies, NGOs, institutions and independent professionals.

The work fits in one sentence: moving an organisation from the stage where someone asks an assistant questions, to the stage where systems actually carry out work. In between there are processes to map, data to connect and teams to train. That is where we come in.
We resell no licences and are tied to no vendor. The model we choose depends on the problem to solve, not on a commercial agreement.
about.groupTitle: A group that uses what it sells
about.groupBody: Most AI agencies have never had to run an AI system under real constraints: traffic, dropped connections, thin margins, users with no time to learn. Rapyogo has. Each service in the group has its own domain, and the artificial intelligence they run is the one we build.

about.founderRole: Founder and CEO of Rapyogo SARL
founderBody: {name} was born and raised in Bukavu. A psychology graduate, he turned to entrepreneurship for a simple reason: that is where he could take on the problems he saw every day.

His first venture, a fast-food outlet, showed him what was wrong with food delivery in the DRC: waste, delays, and a service out of reach for people with reduced mobility. In 2023 he launched Rapyogo Food — now Viteat — to answer it: dark kitchens, a dedicated fleet, electric motorbikes, and AI running dispatch.

As a person with albinism in a society where that still invites prejudice, he made inclusion a design criterion rather than a talking point: the group's products are built first for the people standard services leave out.

RAPIA grew out of that path. A psychology background is no detour for an AI agency: most projects fail not on the technology, but because nobody looked at how a team actually works before handing it a tool.

faq.metaTitle: Frequently asked questions about AI adoption
faq.metaDescription: Cost, timelines, data security, limited connectivity, team training: direct answers to the questions Congolese organisations ask before an artificial intelligence project.
faq.heading: What people ask us before we start
faq.subtitle: The questions raised in a first meeting, with the answers we actually give.

items.question: Do we need to be "ready" for AI first?
items.answer: No. A ready organisation is one that has already done the work — mapped its processes, tidied its data, identified its bottlenecks. That work is exactly what we do first. What you need at the start is not technical maturity: it is one specific task that costs someone time, every week.

items.question: How much does an artificial intelligence project cost?
items.answer: We publish no price list, because a process audit, a team training session and the implementation of a connected agent share neither duration nor deliverable. Cost depends on three things: how many processes are involved, the state of the data to connect, and the level of autonomy you are aiming for. A one-hour scoping call is enough to establish an order of magnitude before any commitment.

items.question: How long before we see a result?
items.answer: Team training has an effect within the following week: people stop using AI as a search engine. An assistant connected to the organisation's documents usually takes a few weeks, most of the delay coming from data access rather than development. End-to-end automation is deployed in stages, starting with the most expensive process.

items.question: Will our data leave the organisation?
items.answer: That is an architecture decision, not a given. Depending on how sensitive the data is, a solution can run on hosted models, on models operated in a closed environment, or by separating what leaves from what stays. We document that choice before building: you must know which data goes where, and be able to justify it to your board or your donor.

items.question: Will AI replace our team?
items.answer: Our work is to remove tasks, not people. The processes we automate are the ones nobody claims: re-entry, sorting, chasing, formatting, consolidating reports. An organisation that deploys AI to cut headcount loses the only people able to supervise the systems it has just installed.

items.question: What is the difference between using ChatGPT and what you install?
items.answer: A public assistant answers from what it knows in general. It knows neither your procedures, nor your contracts, nor your customer history, and it cannot execute anything in your tools. We distinguish three levels: chatting, connecting — the AI reaches your data and your systems — and delegating, where agents carry out complete tasks under human supervision. Value appears from the second level onwards.

items.question: Does this work with limited internet connectivity?
items.answer: Yes, provided it is designed for from the start. The solutions we build are sized for irregular bandwidth: batched rather than continuous processing, lightweight interfaces, tolerance to outages, and lossless resumption when the connection returns. In the DRC this is a structural constraint, not an edge case.

items.question: Which tools and models do you use?
items.answer: We are agnostic. Depending on the problem, a solution may rely on models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, on hosted open models, or on a combination of all three. The choice is justified by the need — confidentiality, cost per request, language, latency — and documented. A provider who proposes the same tool to every client is selling their partnership, not your outcome.

items.question: Do you train teams too, or only executives?
items.answer: Both, and separately. An executive needs to know how to decide: where to invest, which risks to accept, how to measure. An operational team needs to know how to do it, on their own files. The same material served to both audiences works for neither. RAPIA Academy covers both formats.

items.question: Do you work outside Goma?
items.answer: Yes. We are based in Goma, Kinshasa and Lubumbashi, and we work remotely with organisations elsewhere in the DRC and across the continent. Scoping and training phases benefit from being held on site; the rest is delivered remotely with no loss of quality.

servicesPage.heading: Four ways into the subject
servicesPage.subtitle: Most organisations don't need all four. They need the one that unblocks their situation — and to know which one that is.
intro: An AI engagement is easy to sell and hard to deliver. The difference rarely comes down to technology: it comes down to what was understood about the real work before starting.
So here, for each service, is what it solves, what you get at the end, and who it is for. If your situation fits none of these boxes, tell us: that is useful information, not a problem.

items.problem: Everyone in the organisation is talking about AI and nobody knows where to start. Initiatives head off in four directions, none lands, and management ends up concluding that "it doesn't work here".
delivers: A map of your processes, with the time each one actually consumes
The list of tasks where AI changes something — and those where it adds nothing
A roadmap costed in effort, ordered by expected gain
The risks identified: sensitive data, dependencies, points of failure
items.forWhom: Executive management, operations directors, programme coordination. Any organisation that has to weigh a budget before spending it.

items.problem: The tools are there, the accounts are open, and teams use them like a search engine. The gap between what AI can do and what it is asked to do stays exactly where it was.
delivers: Sessions built on your own files, not on generic examples
Written working methods, reusable after the trainer leaves
A separate level for executives and for operational teams
A remote check-in after the training
items.forWhom: Administrative, finance, HR, communications and coordination teams. Executives who must decide without being technicians.

items.problem: A public assistant knows neither your procedures, nor your contracts, nor your history. Every answer has to be reworked by hand, and the time saved is lost again in checking.
delivers: An assistant connected to your documents and data, with its sources cited
A documented architecture: which data goes where, and why
Recovery after a dropped connection, designed in from the start
Handover to your team, or maintenance if you prefer
items.forWhom: Organisations with real document volume: NGOs, professional firms, institutions, companies with written procedures.

items.problem: Tasks nobody claims eat entire days: re-entry, sorting, chasing, formatting, consolidating reports. They appear in no job description and cost the most.
delivers: Agents that carry out a complete process, under human supervision
The checkpoints where a human approves before anything goes out
A log of what was done, auditable after the fact
Staged deployment, starting with the most expensive process
items.forWhom: Organisations that have already connected their data and want to move from assistance to execution.

trainingPage.heading: Training the people who will work with AI
trainingPage.subtitle: An organisation does not become more effective because it bought licences. It becomes effective when its teams know what to do with them.
intro: Most AI training runs on invented examples: drafting a fictional letter, summarising an article nobody cares about. Participants leave impressed and change nothing about their Monday.
Our sessions start from your real files. What gets produced during the training is work you will not have to do afterwards — the only indicator that strikes us as serious.
